# Interpolation Schemes for Volume Rendering

Also called: Fourier window, Interpolation Methods, Interpolation Schemes for Frequency Domain Volume Rendering, Nearest Neighbor Interpolation, Reconstruction Filters, Sample-and-hold, Zeroth-order interpolation

## Overview
Interpolation schemes determine how scalar field values are reconstructed from discrete voxel samples during volume ray casting, directly influencing image quality and computational cost [S1, S2, unofficial]. They solve the problem of sampling a continuous volume representation at arbitrary ray positions that rarely align with integer grid coordinates [S4, unofficial]. This family is distinguished from sibling techniques like [Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing via Ray Distribution](1219-multi-sample-anti-aliasing-via-ray-distribution.md) by focusing on the spatial reconstruction kernel rather than the statistical distribution of sample points, and from [Depth to Distance Conversion](2428-depth-to-distance-conversion.md) by operating on the scalar field values rather than geometric depth buffers.

## Shared principles
All interpolation schemes in this family map a query position $\mathbf{p}$ in voxel space to a scalar value $V(\mathbf{p})$ by combining a finite set of neighboring voxel values $V_i$ using a set of weights $w_i(\mathbf{p})$:
$$ V(\mathbf{p}) = \sum_{i} w_i(\mathbf{p}) V_i $$
The weights are derived from a reconstruction kernel $h(\mathbf{z})$, where $\mathbf{z}$ is the distance from the query point to the sample center. The choice of kernel defines the trade-off between computational complexity, spatial extent (number of neighbors), and frequency response (aliasing vs. blurring) [S1, S2, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Frequency Domain Volume Rendering with Sinc Resampling](826-frequency-domain-volume-rendering-with-sinc-resampling.md)
A direct volume ray casting technique that performs resampling in the frequency domain using Fourier transforms to avoid blurring artifacts associated with spatial domain interpolation, particularly for large zoom factors. It exploits signal processing ideas such as the shifting theorem, the packing theorem, and the derivative theorem to achieve the best theoretical quality by using the ideal interpolation filter (sinc). Unlike standard spatial domain filters (e.g., B-spline, Catmull-Rom) or methods that zoom the intermediate image, this method resamples every volume slice in object space before projection, ensuring perfect reconstruction if the sampling meets Nyquist criteria.

### [Fast tri-cubic interpolation](848-fast-tri-cubic-interpolation.md)
A GPU-based higher-order reconstruction scheme that evaluates a tri-cubic B-spline filter by reducing the number of texture fetches required for the convolution sum, leveraging GPU linear filtering capabilities. It solves the performance bottleneck of standard cubic interpolation, which requires 64 texel fetches for a 3D tri-cubic filter, by using separable filter kernels stored in 1D textures and pre-computed weight/offset functions to achieve the same result with only eight tri-linear texture fetches. It differs from [Frequency Domain Volume Rendering with Sinc Resampling](826-frequency-domain-volume-rendering-with-sinc-resampling.md) by operating in the spatial domain using fixed B-spline kernels rather than windowed sinc functions in the frequency domain.

### [Bilinear Interpolation](858-bilinear-interpolation.md)
Estimates values at arbitrary 2D coordinates by linearly interpolating across the four nearest grid points. It sets itself apart from nearest neighbor interpolation by eliminating blocky artifacts while maintaining lower computational cost than higher-order schemes like tri-cubic interpolation.

### [Hardware Interpolation Approximation](1027-hardware-interpolation-approximation.md)
This method approximates volume rendering integration by leveraging standard graphics hardware rasterization, assuming linear interpolation along ray segments. It sets itself apart from analytical integration schemes by relying on the implicit interpolation of the GPU's rasterizer, resulting in view-dependent piecewise bilinear or trilinear interpolation depending on how the hardware subdivides polygons.

### [Trilinear Interpolation](1531-trilinear-interpolation.md)
Estimates the scalar field value at an arbitrary point within a voxel grid by computing a weighted average of the eight surrounding voxel corner values. It solves the problem of sampling continuous volume data at non-integer coordinates, which occurs because ray casting sample points rarely align exactly with voxel centers. Compared to nearest-neighbor interpolation, trilinear interpolation produces significantly smoother images with fewer aliasing artifacts, though it requires approximately five times more computation time.

### [Inverse Distance Weighted Interpolation](2336-inverse-distance-weighted-interpolation.md)
Inverse Distance Weighted (IDW) Interpolation is a spatial interpolation method that generates a continuous 3D scalar field from discrete sample points by weighting nearby samples by the inverse of their distance raised to a power. It solves the problem of reconstructing a volume from irregular or sparse data (e.g., drill-hole assays) where grid-aligned interpolation schemes like trilinear are not directly applicable. Unlike [Trilinear Interpolation](1531-trilinear-interpolation.md), which assumes a regular grid, IDW operates on arbitrary point sets, though it does not guarantee $C^0$ continuity along interior faces of the grid.

### Variable Gaussian Blurring
A reconstruction technique used to reduce visible artifacts from the discrete sampled nature of volume models, specifically false low frequencies caused by the Nyquist limit [S5, unofficial]. It applies variable Gaussian blurring to the source volume models before or during reconstruction to high-resolution 2D images [S5, unofficial]. The Nyquist Limit is defined as half the sampling rate, and infinite sampling of continuous surfaces is the only way to completely avoid artifacts [S5, unofficial].

### Barycentric Color Interpolation for Voxels
Interpolates vertex colors to a voxel center by treating the voxel center as a point inside the triangle and weighting the vertex colors by the areas of the sub-triangles formed with the voxel center [S6, unofficial]. The formula is $c = c_1 (A_2 / A) + c_2 (A_3 / A) + c_3 (A_1 / A)$, where $A_1 = \text{area}(v_1, v_2, P)$, $A_2 = \text{area}(v_2, v_3, P)$, $A_3 = \text{area}(v_3, v_1, P)$, $A = A_1 + A_2 + A_3$, and $P$ is the voxel center [S6, unofficial].

### Adaptive Interpolation for Isosurface Detection
Interpolates input volume along rays at a predetermined sampling rate. It uses non-binary classifiers to adjust the acceptable density range for an isovalue surface based on data change rate [S2, unofficial]. When data values change slowly, a narrow range of acceptable values is used; when data values change rapidly, a wide range is used to avoid missing the surface [S2, unofficial]. It supports user selection of interpolation: nearest-neighbor (preview), linear (day-to-day), cubic (publication-quality) [S2, unofficial].

## Background
The concept of interpolation in volume rendering emerged with the development of direct volume ray casting in the late 1980s. Levoy's foundational work on ray casting introduced the need to sample continuous volume data, initially relying on simple methods [S2, unofficial]. The distinction between zeroth-order (nearest-neighbor), first-order (linear/trilinear), and higher-order (cubic/sinc) interpolation was formalized to address the trade-off between rendering speed and visual fidelity [S1, S2, unofficial]. Nearest-neighbor interpolation, equivalent to convolving with a rect function (sample-and-hold), was identified as a poor low-pass filter due to passband distortion and stopband leakage, leading to aliasing and blockiness [S2, unofficial]. Trilinear interpolation became the standard for real-time applications due to its balance of smoothness and speed, though it introduces $C^1$ discontinuities (star patterns) [S2, S5, unofficial]. Higher-order methods, such as tri-cubic B-splines and windowed sinc filters (e.g., Blackman window of width four), were developed to eliminate these artifacts for publication-quality imagery, albeit at higher computational cost [S3, S4, unofficial]. The introduction of frequency domain rendering techniques in the 1990s and 2000s provided an alternative approach to achieve high-quality sinc-like reconstruction without the spatial domain artifacts [S1, S4, unofficial].
